1	# Bill of Materials — Dark Sky Monitor
2	
3	Chosen parts with the reasoning behind each choice, plus the gotchas that cost a week if missed.
4	Prices are **overestimated** single-unit retail (Oct 2026) — verify current prices before ordering.
5	
6	## STATUS: ORDERED 2026-10-06
7	
8	Everything below is what was actually purchased, which closes the hardware half of M0.
9	
10	| Part | Role | Source | Price |
11	|---|---|---|---|
12	| **Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, 1 GB** (SKU SC0192) — ordered | the computer | PiShop.us (authorized reseller) | $35.00 |
13	| **TSL2591** breakout, 3 V/5 V, I2C | sensor 1 — sky brightness | Amazon (EC Buying) | ~$11 |
14	| **MLX90614 / GY-906, 3.3 V variant** | sensor 2 — zenith IR temperature (cloud) | Amazon (Teyleten Robot) | ~$13 |
15	| **BME280**, 3.3 V, I2C/SPI, includes jumper wires | sensor 3 — ambient temp / humidity / pressure | Amazon | ~$9 |
16	
17	**Three sensors. The DS3231 RTC is a clock, not a sensor** — it measures nothing and is not part of
18	the fusion, but it is still required (offline means no NTP; see Decisions below). **Not yet ordered.**
19	
20	### Why the 1 GB Pi
21	
22	Headless Raspberry Pi OS Lite uses ~300 MB and our workload is a handful of small C daemons at
23	≤1 Hz. More RAM buys nothing here, and DRAM prices are currently elevated — the same store lists the
24	Pi 4 2 GB at $67.50 and the Pi 5 2 GB at $77.50. The 1 GB Pi 4 is also on the spec's approved
25	platform list (§17: any Pi with the 40-pin header).
26	
27	### Why the 3.3 V MLX90614 specifically — this was a real decision, not a preference
28	
29	The GY-906 breakout ties its I2C pull-up resistors to VCC. Powered at 5 V, SDA and SCL sit at 5 V and
30	run straight into Pi GPIO, which has **no 5 V tolerance and no overvoltage protection** (spec §17
31	calls this out as the most popular way to lose a Pi). The listing offered both a 5 V and a 3.3 V
32	pack; we took the **3.3 V** pack so the entire bus stays at 3.3 V.
33	
34	Side effect worth knowing: 3.3 V MLX90614 variants often have a narrower field of view than the 5 V
35	parts. That is acceptable and arguably better — a narrower view of the zenith is less likely to catch
36	a roof edge or tree branch, which would radiate at its own temperature and corrupt ΔT.
37	
38	### Verification checklist — do this the day the parts arrive
39	
40	Results go in [`hardware-log.md`](hardware-log.md). Do all five before writing a line of C.
41	
42	1. `i2cdetect -y 1` → expect **0x29** (TSL2591) and **0x5A** (MLX90614) and **0x76** (BME280).
43	2. **Read the BME280 chip-ID register: `0x60` = genuine BME280, `0x58` = a BMP280 with no humidity
44	   sensor → return it immediately.** The listing claims humidity, but listings are not evidence.
45	3. MLX90614 pointed at open night sky vs. an indoor wall — sky should read tens of °C colder. If they
46	   match, something is in the field of view or the part is bad.
47	4. **The window-material test, which de-risks the project's largest hardware unknown.** Hold acrylic
48	   in front of the MLX90614: the cold-sky reading should disappear, confirming acrylic is opaque in
49	   its 8–14 µm band. Then try thin LDPE film and confirm the cold reading survives.
50	5. TSL2591 at max gain in a sealed dark box — record the dark offset; this is the noise floor every
51	   night-sky reading sits on.
52	
53	### Still to buy
54	
55	| Part | Why | Est. |
56	|---|---|---|
57	| USB-C power supply, 5.1 V 3 A | **The Pi will not boot without it.** Use a real supply, not a phone charger — undervoltage causes instability and SD corruption that looks exactly like a software bug. | $10 |
58	| microSD, high-endurance 32 GB | We write continuously for weeks; dashcam-rated cards exist for this. | $14 |
59	| DS3231 RTC + LIR2032 | Offline timekeeping. Without it the sun/moon ephemeris is impossible. | $7 |
60	| Enclosure, window materials | Home Depot / Lowe's. LDPE film for the IR aperture. | $14 |
61	
62	Jumper wires came bundled with the BME280.
63	
64	---
65	
66	## Decisions
67	
68	### Sky brightness → **TSL2591**
69	
70	| Option | Verdict |
71	|---|---|
72	| **TSL2591** | **Chosen.** 600,000,000:1 dynamic range; minimum detectable ~188 µLux. Programmable gain (up to 9876×) and integration time (up to 600 ms) let us push sensitivity at night. Proven in DIY sky-quality-meter builds. |
73	| TSL2561 | Rejected — older, much narrower dynamic range. |
74	| TSL237 (light-to-frequency) | Rejected *for now*. Its pulse output would make brightness an interrupt-timestamping problem (mechanism B), but at bright levels output approaches MHz and would swamp Pi GPIO interrupts, forcing an adaptive gate-counting design. Harder to source on a breakout. Revisit only if we decide we want B. |
75	| BH1750 / generic lux breakouts | Rejected — ~1 lux resolution floor. Night sky is ~0.001 lux. Off by three orders of magnitude. |
76	
77	**Bonus we get for free:** the TSL2591 has *two* photodiodes — full-spectrum (Ch0) and infrared (Ch1).
78	The Ch0/Ch1 ratio hints at light-*source* type, because moonlight, sodium vapour and LED street
79	lighting have different visible-to-IR ratios. That is a second fusion feature from one sensor, and
80	a good stretch goal.
81	
82	**Honest limit:** a truly dark site reads ~0.0002 lux, right at this sensor's floor. In Fort Collins
83	proper (~0.003 lux) it is comfortable. Mitigation: max gain, 600 ms integration, average many
84	samples, and characterise the dark offset in a sealed box.
85	
86	### Cloud cover → **MLX90614** (wide FOV, 3 V-safe breakout)
87	
88	| Option | Verdict |
89	|---|---|
90	| **MLX90614** | **Chosen.** The standard DIY cloud-sensor part. Object temperature range −70 to +380 °C covers cold sky. I2C. |
91	| MLX90640 (32×24 thermal array) | Rejected — ~$60+, and spatial resolution buys us nothing for a single ΔT measurement. |
92	| AMG8833 (8×8 thermal) | Rejected — $25–40 for spatial data we don't need. |
93	
94	**Buy the Adafruit breakout, not a bare clone.** The clones are where the I2C flakiness stories come
95	from; Adafruit's board includes level shifting and a regulator so it is safe on the Pi's 3.3 V I2C.
96	
97	**Wide field of view is a feature, not a compromise.** The standard part sees ~90°. Cloud cover is
98	inherently a spatial average, so averaging a broad patch of sky is what we actually want. A narrow-FOV
99	variant costs more and is harder to source for no benefit here. Be ready to say this out loud.
100	
101	### Ambient temp / humidity / pressure → **BME280**
102	
103	| Option | Verdict |
104	|---|---|
105	| **BME280** | **Chosen.** The only single chip giving temperature **+ humidity + pressure** on I2C. Humidity is *required* for the ΔT correction; pressure is a free bonus for front detection. |
106	| BMP280 | Rejected — **no humidity sensor.** Humidity is the whole reason this part exists in our design. |
107	| SHT31 / SHT41 | Rejected — better humidity accuracy but no pressure, so we'd need a fourth part. |
108	| DHT22 | Rejected — bit-banged microsecond timing from userspace, slow, coarse. The spec itself lists it as "a lesson in why kernels exist." |
109	
110	### Clock → **DS3231**
111	
112	Required, not optional: no network means **no NTP**, and the Pi has no battery-backed clock. Without
113	it we cannot know whether it is astronomically dark, and the sun/moon ephemeris — the component
114	carrying most of this project's sophistication — is impossible.
115	
116	DS3231 over DS1307 because the DS3231 is temperature-compensated (±2 ppm vs ~±20 ppm) for the same money.
117	
118	### Computer → **Raspberry Pi 4, 2 GB**
119	
120	- **2 GB is plenty.** The workload is three sensors at ≤1 Hz. Do not pay for 4–8 GB.
121	- **Pi 4 over Pi 5** for a concrete reason: the Pi 5 moved GPIO behind a new RP1 chip, which is newer
122	  and less documented. If we attempt mechanism A (a character driver), the Pi 4's better-documented
123	  peripherals matter. The Pi 4 also runs cooler, which matters for a sealed box left outside.
124	- **Pi 4 over Zero 2 W** only because we compile on it. A Zero 2 W would *run* this fine.
125	- A used Pi 4 or 3B+ off Marketplace/eBay (~$35) is a legitimate way to save $20.
126	
127	## The build list
128	
129	| # | Part | Why this exact one | Est. |
130	|---|---|---|---|
131	| 1 | Raspberry Pi 4 (2 GB) | see above | $55 |
132	| 2 | **High-endurance** microSD 32 GB (SanDisk High Endurance / Samsung PRO Endurance) | We write continuously for weeks. These are built for dashcams — continuous writes — and cost ~$3 more than a card that will wear out. 32 GB is plenty. | $14 |
133	| 3 | Official Pi USB-C PSU (5.1 V 3 A) | **Not a phone charger.** Undervoltage on a Pi causes random instability and SD corruption, and it looks exactly like a software bug. Worst possible week to debug. | $10 |
134	| 4 | TSL2591 breakout (Adafruit #1980 or equiv.) | sky brightness | $12 |
135	| 5 | MLX90614 breakout (Adafruit #1747 or equiv.) | cloud via sky IR temperature | $20 |
136	| 6 | BME280 breakout (Adafruit #2652 / SparkFun) | ambient + **humidity** + pressure | $16 |
137	| 7 | DS3231 RTC + CR2032 or LIR2032 | offline timekeeping | $10 |
138	| 8 | Breadboard + female-female jumper wires | prototype before enclosing | $14 |
139	| 9 | IP65 project box / junction box (Home Depot, Lowe's) | enclosure | $14 |
140	| 10 | Clear acrylic or glass scrap (brightness window), thin LDPE film, standoffs, screws | see enclosure notes | $10 |
141	| | **Recommended total** | | **~$175** |
142	
143	### Lean version (~$121, ≈ $60 each)
144	
145	Used Pi 4/3B+ ($35) · SD ($14) · PSU ($10) · TSL2591 clone ($11) · MLX90614 clone ($13) · BME280
146	($9, **verify chip ID**) · DS3231 ($7) · wire kit ($12) · junction box ($10).
147	
148	### Optional, strongly recommended later
149	
150	| Part | Why | Est. |
151	|---|---|---|
152	| Power resistor (~10–22 Ω) + MOSFET + wire | Dew heater for the IR aperture. Turns failure mode #4 into a feature and adds a measurable control loop. | $8 |
153	| 3D-printed sensor shroud | **Ask whether CSU has a makerspace printer** — likely free. | $0 |
154	
155	## Purchasing plan
156	
157	We are **buying and keeping** everything — no loaned or borrowed parts. Two orders, split by whether
158	authenticity matters.
159	
160	### Order 1 — Adafruit (the three sensors + RTC)
161	
162	One order, one shipping fee, all four parts authentic, and every one has a written tutorial and a
163	maintained C/Python library. This is the single most important order to get right, because the
164	sensors are where counterfeits and flaky clones cost whole weeks.
165	
166	| Search Adafruit for | Part # | Est. |
167	|---|---|---|
168	| "TSL2591 High Dynamic Range Digital Light Sensor" | 1980 | $7–11 |
169	| "MLX90614 Contact-less Infrared Thermopile Sensor" | 1747 | $17–20 |
170	| "BME280 I2C or SPI Temperature Humidity Pressure Sensor" | 2652 | $15–17 |
171	| "DS3231 Precision RTC" (breakout or STEMMA QT) | 5188 / 3013 | $7–14 |
172	
173	**Choose USPS Priority Mail at checkout**, not ground — from NYC to Colorado that is roughly 2–3
174	days rather than 4–6, for a few dollars more.
175	
176	**Check SparkFun first anyway** (Niwot, CO — ~45 min from Fort Collins). They definitely stock the
177	BME280, and anything they do carry arrives in 1–2 days in-state. Their catalogue for the TSL2591 /
178	MLX90614 / DS3231 is less certain — if they have them, buy local; otherwise Adafruit covers everything.
179	
180	### Order 2 — Amazon (Pi + commodity hardware)
181	
182	These parts are identical wherever you buy them, so take the fastest shipping.
183	
184	| Search Amazon for | What to pick | Est. |
185	|---|---|---|
186	| "CanaKit Raspberry Pi 4 Starter Kit" or "Vilros Raspberry Pi 4 kit" | A kit bundling the Pi 4 (2 GB or 4 GB), **official-spec USB-C power supply**, case, fan and heatsinks. Buying the kit removes the undervoltage risk and the enclosure question in one click. | $95–120 |
187	| "SanDisk High Endurance microSD 32GB" or "Samsung PRO Endurance 32GB" | **Buy this even though the kit includes a card.** Kit cards are generic and will wear out under continuous logging. Use the kit card as a spare. | $12–15 |
188	| "Dupont female to female jumper wires 20cm" | A 120-wire assortment. Female-to-female connects breakout headers straight to the Pi's GPIO. | $7–9 |
189	| "830 point breadboard" | Prototype before anything goes in a box. | $7 |
190	| "IP65 junction box" / "weatherproof project enclosure" | ~6×4×3 in, hinged lid, cable gland. **Home Depot or Lowe's in person is cheaper and immediate** for this one. | $12–15 |
191	
192	**If a Micro Center is within driving distance of the Front Range, check it first** — they stock
193	Raspberry Pi boards and sensors, and same-day pickup beats any shipping. Worth one phone call.
194	
195	### Buying the Pi separately instead of as a kit
196	
197	Cheaper but more pieces: Pi 4 (2 GB) ~$55 from an authorised reseller (Adafruit, PiShop.us,
198	Chicago Electronic Distributors, Newark) + **official** 5.1 V 3 A USB-C PSU ~$10 + case ~$12. Only do
199	this if the kit price looks inflated — the kit's bundled official-spec PSU is worth real money in
200	avoided debugging.
201	
202	### Verify the day the parts arrive
203	
204	Do all of this before writing a line of C. Each item has cost somebody a week.
205	
206	1. `i2cdetect -y 1` → expect **0x29** (TSL2591), **0x5A** (MLX90614), **0x76** (BME280), **0x68**
207	   (DS3231). Anything missing is a wiring or address problem, not a software problem.
208	2. **Read the BME280's chip-ID register: 0x60 = genuine BME280, 0x58 = a BMP280 with no humidity
209	   sensor.** If it reads 0x58, return it immediately.
210	3. Point the MLX90614 at the open sky on a clear night and at a wall indoors. Expect a sky reading
211	   tens of degrees colder than the wall. If both read about the same, something is in the field of
212	   view or the part is bad.
213	4. **Test the IR window material now.** Hold acrylic in front of the MLX90614 — the cold-sky reading
214	   should vanish, confirming acrylic is opaque in its band. Then try thin LDPE film and confirm the
215	   cold reading survives. This single ten-minute test de-risks the project's largest hardware
216	   unknown.
217	5. Confirm the DS3231 keeps time across a full power-off.
218	
219	### Money
220	
221	Roughly **$150–190 all-in**, so **$75–95 each** split two ways. One partner should place both orders
222	and the other reimburses — splitting an order across two accounts just doubles the shipping.
223	
224	## Gotchas that cost a week if missed
225	
226	1. **Counterfeit BME280s are rampant.** Boards sold as "BME280" are frequently BMP280 (no humidity) —
227	   and humidity is the entire reason we bought it. **Verify by reading the chip-ID register: 0x60 =
228	   BME280, 0x58 = BMP280.** Do this the day the part arrives, not in week 11. Buying from SparkFun or
229	   Adafruit avoids the problem.
230	2. **The MLX90614 cannot see through acrylic.** Acrylic and most plastics are opaque in the 8–14 µm
231	   band it uses, so a sealed clear window **blinds the cloud sensor** — half of our fusion. Options:
232	   an open aperture under an offset rain hood tilted ~15° for drainage, or a **thin LDPE film**
233	   window (polyethylene is reasonably LWIR-transparent — cling film or a bag, calibrated in place,
234	   replaced periodically). **Test this in the first week the part is in hand.**
235	3. **The MLX90614 is finicky on the Pi's hardware I2C** (SMBus repeated-start behaviour). Two fixes,
236	   and the second is better: lower the bus speed (`dtparam=i2c_arm_baudrate=50000` in
237	   `/boot/firmware/config.txt`), **or** put the MLX90614 on its own bit-banged `i2c-gpio` bus on
238	   separate pins. The second option solves two problems at once — it dodges the SMBus quirk *and*
239	   removes this sensor from bus contention with the other three (see the I2C contention discussion in
240	   `design-review.md` §5).
241	4. **Cheap DS3231 modules (ZS-042) have a trickle-charge circuit** intended for a rechargeable
242	   LIR2032. Fitting a non-rechargeable CR2032 means the board tries to charge it — a leak/rupture
243	   risk. Either fit a LIR2032, remove the charging resistor, or buy the Adafruit breakout which
244	   doesn't do this.
245	5. **Keep I2C cable runs under ~30 cm.** I2C is not a long-distance bus; cable capacitance causes
246	   corruption that looks like random sensor failure. If the sensor head must sit further from the Pi,
247	   lower the baudrate and expect to debug it.
248	
249	## Wiring
250	
251	All four devices are I2C and **their addresses do not collide** — worth stating explicitly, because
252	address conflicts are a classic time sink:
253	
254	| Device | Address |
255	|---|---|
256	| TSL2591 | 0x29 |
257	| MLX90614 | 0x5A |
258	| BME280 | 0x76 (or 0x77) |
259	| DS3231 | 0x68 (+ 0x57 if the module carries an AT24C32 EEPROM) |
260	
261	- Power everything from the Pi's **3.3 V** pin where the breakout allows it. Nothing here needs 5 V.
262	- Pi I2C is on **GPIO2 (SDA)** and **GPIO3 (SCL)**, which have built-in 1.8 kΩ pull-ups. Four breakouts
263	  each adding their own pull-ups in parallel lowers the effective resistance; usually fine at 100 kHz,
264	  but if the bus misbehaves this is a place to look.
265	- **Wire with the Pi powered off.** A Pi killed by a hot-plugged jumper in week 11 is a schedule
266	  event, not a hardware event.
267	- Confirm everything enumerates with `i2cdetect -y 1` before writing a line of C.
268	
269	## Enclosure and placement
270	
271	- **Sensor head points at the zenith**, as far from walls, roof overhangs and windows as practical —
272	  anything in the field of view radiates at its own temperature and corrupts ΔT.
273	- **TSL2591:** behind a clear acrylic or glass window. **Calibrate with the window in place** so its
274	  transmission folds into the calibration constant. Note that acrylic yellows under UV over months.
275	- **MLX90614:** open aperture or LDPE film, under an offset hood, tilted ~15° so water runs off.
276	- **BME280:** shaded and vented. Direct sun or trapped case heat makes its temperature reading useless,
277	  and that reading is the ambient reference for every ΔT.
278	- **Pi and RTC:** inside the sealed part of the box. The Pi's own heat is a feature in a Colorado
279	  November.

content.text:
I read everything, ran the three builds (all pass), and changed nothing in the repo. One correction: when I checked `make memcheck`, valgrind left a 20 MB core dump in the repo root. I deleted it, and `git status` is clean again.

I worked from your pasted list of M2 requirements and the spec section numbers cited in the repo. I haven't seen the handout itself, and I didn't open any datasheets.

## 1. Read

I read everything in the order you gave: [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md), [docs/progress-log.md](docs/progress-log.md), [docs/design-review.md](docs/design-review.md), [PROBLEM.md](PROBLEM.md), [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md), [docs/hardware-log.md](docs/hardware-log.md), [docs/bill-of-materials.md](docs/bill-of-materials.md), all of `src/` and `tests/`, plus the README, EVALUATION.md, transcripts/README and the git log.

## 2. Build output (CS machine `topeka`, x86-64 Linux, gcc 16.1.0, not the Pi)

```
$ make
gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -g -O1 -Isrc -Itests -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L src/common/crc32.c src/common/record.c src/store/store.c tests/test_main.c tests/test_crc32.c tests/test_record.c tests/test_store.c -o build/test_all
[exit 0]

$ make test
./build/test_all
116 checks, 0 failed
[exit 0]

$ make asan
rm -rf build
gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -g -O1 -Isrc -Itests -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer src/common/crc32.c src/common/record.c src/store/store.c tests/test_main.c tests/test_crc32.c tests/test_record.c tests/test_store.c -o build/test_all
./build/test_all
116 checks, 0 failed
[exit 0]
```

I also found a Makefile bug. `make asan` leaves a sanitizer-built `build/test_all` behind, and `make memcheck` then runs valgrind on that binary without rebuilding:

```
$ make memcheck   (immediately after make asan)
==2978892==ASan runtime does not come first in initial library list; ...
==2978892== Process terminating with default action of signal 11 (SIGSEGV): dumping core
```

After `make clean && make memcheck`, it's clean:

```
==2978917== All heap blocks were freed -- no leaks are possible
==2978917== ERROR SUMMARY: 0 errors from 0 contexts (suppressed: 0 from 0)
[exit 0]
```

So the store code has now been valgrind-checked on Linux. It has never been tested on the Pi (ARM): the Pi run in the hardware log is the older 15-check build, before the store existed.

## 3. DESIGN.md vs. M2 requirements

[DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) is still the skeleton: every section says **TODO**. The "Where it lives" column says where the source material is.

| Requirement | Status | Where it lives | What's left |
|---|---|---|---|
| Architecture diagram with rates on every arrow | **Missing** (draft in review) | design-review §5 ASCII diagram, §10 process table | Rates appear only inside the sensor boxes, not on any arrow. No threads shown. The only kernel component drawn is "Linux i2c-dev": nothing for shared memory, semaphores, sockets, pipes, `SIGCHLD`, page cache, `fsync` or the SD card. The sensor-to-hub link still reads "SHM ring + sem **or** UDS". The 3-process vs. single-broker question is still open. |
| Mechanism mapping (D, E) | **Missing** (draft in review) | PROBLEM.md "The mechanisms", design-review §10 | The reasons are there, but not in the required form: a measurable requirement → component. Names exist (`stored` for D; `dskyd` + `skyd`/`cloudd`/`envd` + IPC for E), but nothing says how fast a dead sensor must be detected, or how much data a power cut may lose. |
| Failure-mode table | **Partial** in review | design-review §12 (10 rows, all four columns) | It's organized by failure; the requirement is by component. No rows for `stored` failing to open, `fusiond`, the supervisor itself, the IPC ring, SD write errors, BME280/TSL2591 faults, or the CLI/LAN side. The log column says "FAULT record" instead of showing real log lines. Row 9 assumes an RTC we don't have. The "N failures" thresholds aren't set. A child that hangs is never detected (see §4 below). |
| Storage and data | **Partial**; format is real code | progress-log record contract, `store.h`, design-review §8–9 | The 48-byte record and 24-byte header are implemented and tested. Still undecided: retention horizon, `fsync` interval, segment rotation, MANIFEST. Two data rates in the docs disagree (§6). Power-cut-mid-write is designed (truncate at the first bad CRC) but not implemented; today a torn record makes later appends misaligned. |
| Constraints and substitutions | **Missing**, and the stub is wrong | DESIGN.md stub; BOM; design-review §4 | The stub says "the budget forced a 2-sensor build", but we bought 3 sensors. Real substitutions: no RTC, Amazon clones instead of Adafruit, 1 GB Pi, standard 16 GB SD card, no enclosure yet, no reference SQM, no named user, brightness is relative only. |

## 4. Your proposed ownership (mechanism E)

**What it means concretely:**
- **`src/super/` (the supervisor, `dskyd`):**
  - start each child with fork/exec, and detect its death through pipe EOF and `SIGCHLD`/`waitpid`
  - restart with exponential backoff, and mark a sensor `DEAD` after a restart storm
  - clean `SIGTERM` shutdown with meaningful exit codes
  - no fds leaking into children
  - the "heartbeat within 60 s of start" rule from CLAUDE.md, and the hourly soak heartbeat
- **`src/sensors/` (`skyd`, `cloudd`, `envd`):**
  - a thin Linux I2C layer using `ioctl(I2C_RDWR)`
  - pure conversion functions (register bytes → fixed-point values) that build on a Mac
  - per-sensor fault detection
  - producing records per the record contract
  - a Linux-only Makefile split so Nick's Mac build keeps working
- **IPC:** sensors → `fusiond` (shared-memory ring + semaphore), CLI → `fusiond` socket, supervisor pipes. The `fusiond` → `stored` socket sits on the boundary with Nick.
- **At the defense you answer for:**
  - evaluation #7 (`kill -9` ×20: detection latency, restart latency, data gap), #8 (I2C contention jitter) and #3 (CPU/RSS heartbeats)
  - failure rows 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10
  - soak injections at hours 8, 14, 20

**M2 sections you should write first:** Architecture (most of the diagram is processes and IPC), the Mechanism E row, the failure rows for sensors / I2C bus / supervisor / IPC, evaluation rows #3, #7, #8, and the AI-use plan. Nick should write Storage and data, the Mechanism D row, the D failure and evaluation rows (#5, #6), and Constraints (he wrote the BOM). Write the Ownership map together, and share #1 (sample-to-storage latency).

**Decisions in your area that aren't made yet:**
1. **3 sensor processes vs. one `i2cd` broker**, and whether the MLX90614 gets its own bit-banged bus (which also removes it from bus contention). The review says to decide this in the design doc. My recommendation: 3 processes, measure the jitter (eval #8), and name the broker as the fallback with a jitter threshold that triggers it.
2. **Sensor → hub transport.** The review justifies shared memory by "high frequency", but we rejected mechanism F because 1 Hz isn't high-rate. The defense will catch that. Keep the ring, but justify it by **lifetime decoupling**: samples keep flowing while `fusiond` restarts. Still undecided: ring depth, what happens on overrun, and who creates and unlinks the shared memory.
3. **A hung child is never detected.** Pipe EOF only fires when a child dies. A daemon stuck inside an I2C `ioctl` is alive and silent. You need heartbeats over the pipe plus a timeout that triggers `SIGKILL`.
4. **What happens to `seq` on restart.** The contract says "starts at 0, +1 per record". A restarted daemon resets to 0, so "a gap is provable lost data" breaks. Options: a run counter in the record, or a restart record at each start.
5. **DEAD vs. recovering on replug.** Failure row 6 says stop restarting and hold `DEAD`; soak hour 14 expects clean recovery when the sensor is plugged back in. You need a slow re-probe while `DEAD`.
6. **Parameters:** backoff start and cap, storm threshold (N failures in T), consecutive-failure count before `DEAD`, read timeout, heartbeat period.
7. **Who supervises `dskyd`** (systemd `Restart=always`?), and how supervisor HEARTBEAT records reach the single storage writer.
8. **Still open in the progress log:** encode a failed read as a `FAULT` record or as a `SAMPLE` without `VALID`? Which `source_id`s do `fusiond` and the supervisor get? Is the payload table agreed?
9. **I2C bus-lockup recovery:** what userspace can actually do about it.

## 5. Design now vs. needs the hardware

**Can be designed now:** process topology, IPC choices, the supervisor state machine and backoff logic, hang detection, record and store formats, recovery algorithm, failure-detection logic, evaluation methods and targets, ownership, AI-use plan, and conversion code (checked against datasheet worked examples).

**Depends on the hardware.** Everything in the "Assumption" column comes from datasheets or recall; none of it is measured:

| Warm-up | Unknown | Log 30 min from a cold power-on. The time to settle becomes how long records carry the `CALIBRATING` flag. |
| Noise floor | TSL2591 floor ~188 µLux vs. night sky ~0.0002–0.003 lux | hardware-log §5 dark-box offset, plus the spread of readings against a stable target, per sensor. |
| Cloud signal | Clear sky reads 20–40 °C below ambient | hardware-log §3. |

44	    Nota Bene: The term project is done in teams of exactly two. Its shape will feel familiar from
45	the assignments: Claude Code is required, your process is graded from your transcripts, and the
46	whole thing ends with a live demonstration and an individual defense in which each of you answers

48	You will choose a user, choose their problem, and build a working device that solves it, subject
49	to the guardrails in Section 3. And one of those guardrails deserves top billing, because it inverts
50	the assignments’ arrangement: Claude Code is required in your workflow and forbidden
51	in your product. Every line of intelligence that runs on the Pi, every decision, detection, and
52	diagnosis, must be code you wrote and can defend. The agent helps you build the machine. It is
53	not allowed to be the machine.

56	1 Overview
57	Every assignment in this course hands you a problem and asks for a program. The term project
58	reverses the polarity. It hands you a program-shaped hole in the world and asks you to find it. You
59	will design and build a working device (a Raspberry Pi, at least two sensors, and software of your
60	own) that does something a specific person actually needs done. Not a demo of a sensor. Not a
61	tutorial, reassembled. A device that could sit on a shelf in that person’s life and earn its electricity.
62	    The question that will follow you through this project, from the first memo to the final defense,
63	is this: who wants this, and why doesn’t a phone app already solve it? The second half of that
64	question is quietly load-bearing. A phone runs its apps when someone is looking at it. Your
65	device has to be awake at 3 a.m., unattended, on the day the interesting thing finally happens.
66	Always-on, physically embedded, resource-constrained, unsupervised: that’s exactly the territory
67	where processes, schedulers, interrupts, storage, and IPC stop being lecture topics and start being
68	the difference between a product and a demo. You don’t need to bolt operating-systems content
69	onto this project. Choose an honest problem and the operating-systems content will come to you.
70	Uninvited, and usually at inconvenient hours. The guardrails in Section 3 exist only to make sure
71	the problem you choose is honest.
72	    The project is deliberately open. The five concepts in Section 4 are seeds for your ideation,
73	not a menu to order from; the strongest projects most years are ideas we didn’t think of. What
74	is not open is the standard of evidence. Your system must survive 48 hours unattended and prove
75	it with logs. Your claims about latency, throughput, and reliability must be measurements, not
76	adjectives. And at the end, each of you, separately, must be able to stand in front of your own code
77	and explain why it is the way it is. What is not expected is perfection, and Section 5 says so at
78	length. The world your device ships into is imperfect. Your budget is finite, your sensors are cheap,
79	and the project is graded accordingly: on what you did with what you had, and on the honesty of
80	the accounting.

92	        Grading methodology and the demo you can’t rehearse
93	        The term project accounts for 10% of your course grade and is graded out of
94	        100 points, split the same way the assignments are: most of the points answer a
95	        question the artifacts can settle, and the rest answer a question only you can.
96	        70 points attach to the work and its evidence: the problem memo (5), the design
97	        document (10), the checkpoint demonstration (10), the final system with its 48-
98	        hour soak test (30), and the quantitative evaluation report (15). These are graded
99	        from things we can run, read, and re-measure.
100	        The remaining 30 points are individual, and no teammate can earn them for
101	        you. 10 points come from the analysis of your Claude Code transcripts, on the
102	        same five-level, repository-corroborated scale used in the assignments. 20 points
103	        come from the demo-day defense: questions about lines of your own subsystems,
104	        one question from across the ownership boundary, a defense of one episode from
105	        your PROMPTLOG.md, and a small live modification you make to your own code,
106	        alone, at the keyboard, while we watch. So two partners can submit one flawless
107	        repository and still leave demo day with very different grades. The defense was
108	        never grading the repository. It was grading each of you.
109	        Why the split? Same reason as the assignments, scaled up. A device that works is
110	        a nice thing to have. But a pair of engineers who can each explain, unprompted,
111	        why their sampler can’t drop a reading and what their watchdog does when a
112	        sensor gets unplugged? That’s a nice thing to become, and it’s the thing this
113	        course is actually for.

116	2 Learning Objectives
117	• Translate a real user’s real problem into a system design, and defend every component of that
118	  design by the problem’s demands rather than by habit.
119	• Build an embedded sensing product on Linux that exercises at least two below-the-application-
120	  layer mechanisms: device drivers, interrupt handling, real-time scheduling, custom storage, or

126	• Evaluate a system quantitatively: design the experiments, take the measurements, and present

153	3 The Guardrails: What “Non-Trivial” Means Here
154	An open-ended project needs a floor, or the path of least resistance becomes a Python script that
155	polls a sensor and prints a number. Five guardrails define the floor. Everything above them is
156	yours.
157	
158	3.1 Two sensors that cooperate
159	Your device must incorporate at least two physically distinct sensors, and they must cooperate: fused
160	into one decision, correlated against each other, or feeding a single shared pipeline whose behavior
161	depends on both. Two independent demos stapled together at the README do not satisfy this
162	requirement. That’s one sensor short of the assignment, twice. Cooperation is also where the
163	systems content hides. Two sensors almost never want the same sampling rate, the same interface,
164	or the same latency budget, and reconciling those differences inside one program is the first real
165	design problem this project hands you.

257	3.4 Survivability: the 48-hour soak
258	In the week before demos, your final build must run unattended for at least 48 continuous hours,
259	and the logs proving it are a graded deliverable. The logs must show: a timestamped startup; a
260	heartbeat at least hourly recording process liveness, resident memory (RSS), and cumulative event
261	counts; at least one injected fault during the run (physically unplug a sensor for ten minutes, or
262	kill -9 a sensor process) with the system’s detection, degradation, and recovery visible in the
263	log; and an orderly state at the end.
264	    Understand what this guardrail is really doing. Surviving two days unattended is an operating-
265	systems problem wearing a scheduling-your-week costume. It’s the slow memory leak. The unhan-
266	dled error on the path you never tested. The log that fills the SD card, the child process that dies
267	silently at hour 31, and the watchdog you will be very glad you wrote. A system that dazzles for
268	the five minutes someone is watching and decays the moment they leave has a name: demo. This
269	project is asking for the other thing.

289	4 Ideation
290	This is where the project actually begins, so it gets more room than any other section. I am
291	including 5 worked seeds. But they are seeds, not a menu: none is required, all are claimable by any
292	team, and the strongest proposals most years are ideas we didn’t think of. Read the seeds less for
293	their subjects than for their skeleton. Every one of them has the same bones if you will: an absent
294	observer, an always-on device, intelligence a threshold couldn’t provide, and a user you could name.
295	Your job is to find a problem with the same skeleton and a different flesh.
296	
297	4.1 Three ways to find your own
298	Audit a week. Carry a note for one week and write down every time you, or someone near/close-to
299	you, utters one of two sentences: “I wish I knew. . . ” and “by the time I noticed. . . ”. These are
300	sensor products wearing plain clothes. The first names a measurement that is absent. The second
301	names a measurement that existed but had nobody watching it, which is the 3 a.m. test passing
302	itself, unprompted, in ordinary conversation. A week of honest auditing typically yields a dozen
303	candidates, of which two survive the guardrails. And that’s exactly as many as you need.
304	    Shrink an industry. Predictive maintenance, cold-chain monitoring, occupancy analytics, preci-
305	sion agriculture, structural health monitoring: entire companies exist to do each of these at scale,
306	which means someone has already established, expensively, that the problem is worth solving. Take
307	one. Shrink it to a single machine, a single room, a single shelf, and you inherit a validated problem
308	sized for a semester. You also inherit something rarer: the discovery, which tends to stay with
309	people, that the distance between a course project and a real industry is mostly a matter of scale,
310	not of kind.
311	    Instrument a devotion. Hobbies are problems folks have volunteered for: fermentation, aquari-
312	ums, climbing training, beekeeping, film-developing chemistry, model rocketry. Devotees make the
313	best users, for three reasons that matter to your grade. They already measure things by hand, so the
314	value of automating the measurement is pre-established. They will actually run your device. And
315	they will tell you (at length and for free) exactly what it gets wrong, which is the most expensive
316	kind of feedback in all of engineering; that is now available here for the price of listening.
317	    Whatever you find, run it through the guardrails of Section 3 as filters, and through Section 5
318	as a reality check. Ideally before the memo. Certainly before the design document.

320	4.2 Seed 1: “Is my elderly parent okay today?” (ambient wellness monitor)
321	The user is an adult child who lives an hour, or a continent, away from a parent who lives alone.
322	The moment the product exists for is a quiet one: not the fall, but the morning that didn’t follow

330	answer asks the parent to do something. Wear the pendant. Charge the watch. Answer the daily
331	check-in. And the failure mode is that the people most at risk are precisely the people least likely to
332	keep doing it. The design brief is then a device that demands nothing: no camera, no microphone,

336	    Engineering: a PIR motion sensor and a door or pressure sensor, learning a household’s rhythm.
337	The intelligence (all of it yours) is per-hour activity histograms over a rolling window of weeks, a
338	deviation score that knows a Tuesday from a Sunday, and alert hysteresis. Because the real analytical
339	problem here isn’t detection. It’s restraint. A monitor that cries wolf twice gets unplugged. An
340	unplugged monitor is worse than none, because somebody far away believes it’s on duty. Natural
341	mechanisms: E, because a silently dead wellness monitor is this product’s own nightmare scenario,
342	which makes process isolation and supervision requirements rather than garnish; and D, because
343	weeks of learned baseline must survive a power cut. A scoped-down version that still clears every
344	bar: one room, one rhythm, two weeks of baseline, and an alert log you evaluate for false-alarm

347	4.3 Seed 2: “Why does my sourdough / homebrew / greenhouse keep failing?”
348	    (environmental coach)
349	The user is a devotee (Section 4.1, third method) whose batches keep dying and who has already
350	tried the obvious: a thermometer that’s glanced at while awake. The insight the product is built on
351	is that what kills the batch is almost never the moment anyone is looking. It’s the 4 a.m. excursion.
352	The slow weekend drift. The heater that quietly began short-cycling on Tuesday. And the user’s
353	real question is never “what is the temperature?”; it’s “what is wrong?” The distance between those
354	two questions, between a reading and a diagnosis, is exactly the distance your intelligence has to
355	cover. No threshold covers it.
356	    Engineering: temperature/humidity plus light or CO2 , sampled at rates that differ by an order of
357	magnitude, flowing through a storage layer of your own design (D), often behind a no-drop pipeline
358	(F). The intelligence is rolling statistics, rate-of-change detection, and, the satisfying part, signature
359	detection. A short-cycling heater oscillates with a period and amplitude you can measure. A failing
360	seal shows up as indoor humidity coupling to the outdoor weather. A dying yeast culture flattens
361	a CO2 curve that should be climbing. Encoding that physics into diagnostic rules requires actually
362	learning the domain. Which means talking to your user, which is the job. Where it bites: the
363	temptation to promise twelve diagnoses and deliver them all vaguely. Three diagnoses, each with a
364	measured true- and false-positive rate against failure episodes you provoked on purpose, is the far
365	stronger project. And Section 5 is about why provoking them on purpose is not a workaround but
366	a method.

376	4.4 Seed 3: “Did something happen while I was gone?” (explainable security
377	    node)
378	Everyone with a door has asked the question. The commercial answer is four hours of footage
379	nobody will ever watch. This product’s differentiator is one word: explainable. It answers with a
380	timeline (3:12 p.m., something person-sized, eleven seconds, moving away) that a human can read
381	in five seconds and interrogate afterward. The user is anyone who wants that answer without
382	becoming a security-camera hobbyist and, not incidentally, without pointing an internet-connected
383	lens at their own life. Like Seed 1, the absence of a camera is a feature you can defend out loud.
384	     Engineering: PIR motion plus ultrasonic ranging in an interrupt-driven pipeline. That’s mech-
385	anism B, with the polling comparison built into your evaluation, and usually C, because ranging
386	an object during a two-second event is a latency budget you have to actually meet rather than
387	merely admire. The intelligence is fusion (motion says something, range says how big and how
388	far ), debouncing, event segmentation, and the design of the timeline itself. A log schema from
389	which a human can reconstruct the truth is a genuine engineering artifact, and it’s the thing your
390	demo-day answer to “was that the cat?” will be read from. Speaking of the cat: it is this seed’s
391	honest adversary, and a magnetic reed switch on the door is the cheapest ground-truth generator
392	you will ever wire. Every real entry gets a free label. Scoped-down version: three event classes
393	(person-sized, small, unknown) classified honestly, with the confusion matrix to prove it, beats ten
394	classes classified wishfully.

396	4.5 Seed 4: “Is this machine about to break?” (small-shop predictive mainte-
397	    nance)
398	There is an entire industry (vibration analysis, condition monitoring) built on the fact that machines
399	announce their failures early, in frequencies, to anyone equipped to listen. Its instruments cost more
400	than your car. Its customers are factories. The user here is everyone below that line: the shop with
401	one compressor, the makerspace with one 3-D printer, the laundromat, the house with a furnace
402	fan. The moment the product exists for is the new noise that started on a Tuesday when nobody
403	was in the room. We tend to light up on discovering that the hobby-scale version of a real industry
404	fits inside one semester and about $18 in parts. That discovery is worth having. And nothing says
405	it has to expire with the course.
406	     Engineering: an accelerometer (the MPU-6050’s hardware FIFO is your friend) and a tempera-
407	ture sensor. Mechanism F is nearly mandatory, because a dropped sample corrupts the spectrum;
408	this is the seed where the systems work and the analysis work hold each other honest most tightly.
409	C is close behind, and A is there for the ambitious. The intelligence is feature extraction (FFT
410	band energies, RMS trends) compared against a healthy baseline you recorded yourself. Where it
411	bites, instructively: you can’t wait a semester for a real bearing to fail. So you induce faults. Tape
412	a washer to a fan blade for imbalance. Loosen a mounting bolt. Run the printer with a dry rod.
413	Record labeled captures of each. That’s not cheating; it’s how the real industry builds its test sets,
414	and Section 5 makes it doctrine. The scoped-down version is also simply the honest one: “detects
415	the three faults I can induce on this machine, with these error rates” survives a defense. “Predicts
416	failure” does not.

426	The user is whoever answers for a room that other people complain about: the practice-space
427	manager, the lab steward, the roommate whose name is on the lease. The complaints arrive in the
428	past tense. “It was freezing in here yesterday morning.” “It gets stuffy every afternoon.” And no live
429	dashboard on earth answers a past-tense question. The product is a memory for a building: several
430	sensors, a history, and an interface that can answer “mean CO2 by hour, weekdays, last month” in
431	less time than the argument takes.
432	    Engineering: three or more sensors (air quality, sound level, temperature) as isolated processes
433	feeding a hub over IPC. That’s mechanism E, with real supervision, since a facilities record with a
434	three-day hole has lost the argument it exists to win. Everything persists through a storage layer
435	(D) whose retention, rollup, and fsync policies you must actually decide rather than inherit. The
436	intelligence is the query engine: time-range selection, aggregation, alignment of multi-rate series,
437	and cross-sensor correlation (afternoon CO2 tracking the sound level is an occupancy story told by
438	two sensors that never met). Where it bites: interface ambition. Resist the pretty web app. A crisp
439	CLI with five query verbs and exact semantics is more defensible, and far more extensible at the
440	live-modification station on demo day, than a dashboard with none. This is the seed for teams who
441	suspect they might enjoy building databases, because it is one, in miniature, standing on an IPC
442	layer they also built.

445	5 Building in an Imperfect World
446	Somewhere between the memo and the checkpoint, every team hits the same wall. It’s worth telling
447	you now that the wall is scheduled. The sensor your design really wants is a $400 thermal imager
448	and your budget is $60. The $4 accelerometer you bought instead has a noise floor sitting exactly
449	where the interesting signal lives. The CO2 sensor needs three minutes to warm up and drifts with
450	the weather. And the data you need at the scale you want (a year of failing compressors, a winter of
451	greenhouse nights, 104 labeled door events) does not exist, can’t be bought, and won’t be gathered
452	in one semester by one device on one shelf. None of this means you chose the wrong project! It
453	means the project has become real. Engineering has been called the art of the possible. The phrase
454	is not a consolation; it’s the job description. The constraints are not in the way of the work. They
455	are the medium the work is done in.
456	    The unproductive response is to stare at what can’t be done. The productive one is to ask,
457	repeatedly and in roughly this order, what can:
458	• Substitute. Downgrade the sensor; keep the problem. A PIR and a door switch see more of a
459	  household’s rhythm than you’d guess a thermal camera was needed for. A microphone’s RMS
460	  level is a serviceable occupancy proxy. And two cheap sensors that corroborate each other
461	  routinely outperform one expensive one standing alone. Notice that “corroborate each other” is
462	  Section 3.1 arriving early, wearing a budget. Record in the design document what you wanted,
463	  what you used, and what the substitution costs in capability.
464	• Make your own ground truth. You can’t wait for the bearing to fail, so you provoke the conditions
465	  and label the recordings: the taped washer, the loosened bolt, the greenhouse vent propped open

841	    Startups are rarely founded on a dazzling idea. They are founded on a problem somebody
842	already has and is already solving badly; usually with a spreadsheet and a bad habit. Finding one
843	of those is the hard part, and you were made to do it in Week 5, in front of a skeptical reader. Your
844	problem memo is structurally the opening of a pitch: who the user is, what the problem costs them,
845	why the obvious answer fails, and what you propose instead. The same questions get asked later in
846	nicer rooms with worse coffee.
847	    The next thing you have is rarer than you’d guess. An enormous quantity of software talent
848	can wrap a web API and call it a company. Much less of it can make a physical thing stay alive,
849	unattended, in a stranger’s basement, through a power blip and a sensor that quietly fell off in
850	March. That is a real barrier to entry, and you now have 48 hours of logs saying you cleared it.
851	    You also have evidence. When a customer or an investor asks the only question that matters
852	(“does it work?”), most people answer with adjectives. You can answer with a measured false-
853	positive rate and a limitations section you wrote when nobody was forcing you to be honest. That
854	habit will outlive every technology named in this handout.
855	    Now the part I owe you. The distance from a working prototype to a shippable product is
856	long: sourcing, enclosures, certification if you emit anything interesting, unit economics, a support
857	inbox somebody has to read on a Sunday. No device survives contact with 50 strangers unchanged.
858	Assume version two exists before version one leaves the bench.
859	    But if you are ever going to try this, the cheapest moment of your life is now! You have no
860	payroll and no mortgage. Plus there’s a campus stuffed with resources you are already paying for:
861	the institute for entrepreneurship, pitch competitions, prototyping space, an IP office, faculty who
862	will read your business plan for the price of asking nicely. You also have a co-founder (in your
863	teammate) whose code you have already reviewed for fifteen weeks, which is more due diligence
864	than most founding teams ever manage on each other.
865	    And if the answer turns out to be no? That is a perfectly good answer. You will still have built
866	a real thing for a real person, which was the point the entire time. My door is open either way.

992	Quick flag: anything marked (!) has 5V lurking in it somewhere, so treat those interfaces with a
993	little extra respect.
994	     Here’s the thing about the Pi’s GPIO pins: they only speak 3.3V logic, and there’s zero over-
995	voltage protection built in. Feed one a 5V signal directly and it can just... die. Silently. No warning
996	light, no smoke, sometimes not even a clue until you notice nothing’s responding anymore. And
997	sometimes it doesn’t stop at the pin, it takes the whole SoC down with it. That’s exactly why the
998	HC-SR04 needs a voltage divider on its echo line. The trigger pin is fine with 5V, but the echo pin is
999	not, and if you wire them the same way because “eh, they’re both just signal pins,” congratulations,
1000	you’ve found the single most popular way to lose a Pi in Week 13.
1001	     But power-rail mistakes are even less forgiving. Swap VCC and GND, or let a 5V rail touch the
1002	3.3V rail while you’re poking around with a multimeter, and your board usually doesn’t warn you
1003	first. It just stops working. No gradual decline, no second chances.
1004	     So here’s the move: build anything 5V-adjacent on a breadboard first. Check your voltages
1005	with a meter before the Pi ever gets plugged in. And always, always wire things up with the board
1006	powered off.

                                                    1
 CS 370: Operating Systems
Department of Computer Science                  URL: http://www.cs.colostate.edu/~cs370
Colorado State University                                        Professor: Shrideep Pallickara

    Nota Bene: The term project is done in teams of exactly two. Its shape will feel familiar from
the assignments: Claude Code is required, your process is graded from your transcripts, and the
whole thing ends with a live demonstration and an individual defense in which each of you answers
for the code with your name on it. What’s different is the problem. Nobody hands you this one.
You will choose a user, choose their problem, and build a working device that solves it, subject
to the guardrails in Section 3. And one of those guardrails deserves top billing, because it inverts
the assignments’ arrangement: Claude Code is required in your workflow and forbidden
in your product. Every line of intelligence that runs on the Pi, every decision, detection, and
diagnosis, must be code you wrote and can defend. The agent helps you build the machine. It is
not allowed to be the machine.


1 Overview
Every assignment in this course hands you a problem and asks for a program. The term project
reverses the polarity. It hands you a program-shaped hole in the world and asks you to find it. You
will design and build a working device (a Raspberry Pi, at least two sensors, and software of your
own) that does something a specific person actually needs done. Not a demo of a sensor. Not a
tutorial, reassembled. A device that could sit on a shelf in that person’s life and earn its electricity.
    The question that will follow you through this project, from the first memo to the final defense,
is this: who wants this, and why doesn’t a phone app already solve it? The second half of that
question is quietly load-bearing. A phone runs its apps when someone is looking at it. Your
device has to be awake at 3 a.m., unattended, on the day the interesting thing finally happens.
Always-on, physically embedded, resource-constrained, unsupervised: that’s exactly the territory
where processes, schedulers, interrupts, storage, and IPC stop being lecture topics and start being
the difference between a product and a demo. You don’t need to bolt operating-systems content
onto this project. Choose an honest problem and the operating-systems content will come to you.
Uninvited, and usually at inconvenient hours. The guardrails in Section 3 exist only to make sure
the problem you choose is honest.
    The project is deliberately open. The five concepts in Section 4 are seeds for your ideation,
not a menu to order from; the strongest projects most years are ideas we didn’t think of. What
is not open is the standard of evidence. Your system must survive 48 hours unattended and prove
it with logs. Your claims about latency, throughput, and reliability must be measurements, not
adjectives. And at the end, each of you, separately, must be able to stand in front of your own code
and explain why it is the way it is. What is not expected is perfection, and Section 5 says so at
length. The world your device ships into is imperfect. Your budget is finite, your sensors are cheap,
and the project is graded accordingly: on what you did with what you had, and on the honesty of
the accounting.




                                              Page 2 of 26
 CS 370: Operating Systems
Department of Computer Science               URL: http://www.cs.colostate.edu/~cs370
Colorado State University                                     Professor: Shrideep Pallickara



        Grading methodology and the demo you can’t rehearse
        The term project accounts for 10% of your course grade and is graded out of
        100 points, split the same way the assignments are: most of the points answer a
        question the artifacts can settle, and the rest answer a question only you can.
        70 points attach to the work and its evidence: the problem memo (5), the design
        document (10), the checkpoint demonstration (10), the final system with its 48-
        hour soak test (30), and the quantitative evaluation report (15). These are graded
        from things we can run, read, and re-measure.
        The remaining 30 points are individual, and no teammate can earn them for
        you. 10 points come from the analysis of your Claude Code transcripts, on the
        same five-level, repository-corroborated scale used in the assignments. 20 points
        come from the demo-day defense: questions about lines of your own subsystems,
        one question from across the ownership boundary, a defense of one episode from
        your PROMPTLOG.md, and a small live modification you make to your own code,
        alone, at the keyboard, while we watch. So two partners can submit one flawless
        repository and still leave demo day with very different grades. The defense was
        never grading the repository. It was grading each of you.
        Why the split? Same reason as the assignments, scaled up. A device that works is
        a nice thing to have. But a pair of engineers who can each explain, unprompted,
        why their sampler can’t drop a reading and what their watchdog does when a
        sensor gets unplugged? That’s a nice thing to become, and it’s the thing this
        course is actually for.


2 Learning Objectives
• Translate a real user’s real problem into a system design, and defend every component of that
  design by the problem’s demands rather than by habit.
• Build an embedded sensing product on Linux that exercises at least two below-the-application-
  layer mechanisms: device drivers, interrupt handling, real-time scheduling, custom storage, or
  multi-process architectures with fault isolation.
• Write the product’s intelligence yourself (statistics, signal processing, state machines, control)
  and know precisely why a threshold wouldn’t have sufficed.
• Engineer for unattended operation: supervision, recovery, log discipline, resource stability over

3 The Guardrails: What “Non-Trivial” Means Here
An open-ended project needs a floor, or the path of least resistance becomes a Python script that
polls a sensor and prints a number. Five guardrails define the floor. Everything above them is
yours.

3.1 Two sensors that cooperate
Your device must incorporate at least two physically distinct sensors, and they must cooperate: fused
into one decision, correlated against each other, or feeding a single shared pipeline whose behavior
depends on both. Two independent demos stapled together at the README do not satisfy this
requirement. That’s one sensor short of the assignment, twice. Cooperation is also where the
systems content hides. Two sensors almost never want the same sampling rate, the same interface,
or the same latency budget, and reconciling those differences inside one program is the first real
design problem this project hands you.

3.4 Survivability: the 48-hour soak
In the week before demos, your final build must run unattended for at least 48 continuous hours,
and the logs proving it are a graded deliverable. The logs must show: a timestamped startup; a
heartbeat at least hourly recording process liveness, resident memory (RSS), and cumulative event
counts; at least one injected fault during the run (physically unplug a sensor for ten minutes, or
kill -9 a sensor process) with the system’s detection, degradation, and recovery visible in the
log; and an orderly state at the end.
    Understand what this guardrail is really doing. Surviving two days unattended is an operating-
systems problem wearing a scheduling-your-week costume. It’s the slow memory leak. The unhan-
dled error on the path you never tested. The log that fills the SD card, the child process that dies
silently at hour 31, and the watchdog you will be very glad you wrote. A system that dazzles for
the five minutes someone is watching and decays the moment they leave has a name: demo. This
project is asking for the other thing.

And the last guardrail is the one that shapes all the others: your project must serve a specific user
with a specific problem. This should be named in your problem memo (Section 7) and defensible at
the walkthrough. “People who might want to monitor things” is not a user. Your roommate whose

4 Ideation
This is where the project actually begins, so it gets more room than any other section. I am
including 5 worked seeds. But they are seeds, not a menu: none is required, all are claimable by any
team, and the strongest proposals most years are ideas we didn’t think of. Read the seeds less for
their subjects than for their skeleton. Every one of them has the same bones if you will: an absent
observer, an always-on device, intelligence a threshold couldn’t provide, and a user you could name.
Your job is to find a problem with the same skeleton and a different flesh.

4.1 Three ways to find your own
Audit a week. Carry a note for one week and write down every time you, or someone near/close-to
you, utters one of two sentences: “I wish I knew. . . ” and “by the time I noticed. . . ”. These are
sensor products wearing plain clothes. The first names a measurement that is absent. The second
names a measurement that existed but had nobody watching it, which is the 3 a.m. test passing
itself, unprompted, in ordinary conversation. A week of honest auditing typically yields a dozen
candidates, of which two survive the guardrails. And that’s exactly as many as you need.
    Shrink an industry. Predictive maintenance, cold-chain monitoring, occupancy analytics, preci-
sion agriculture, structural health monitoring: entire companies exist to do each of these at scale,
which means someone has already established, expensively, that the problem is worth solving. Take
one. Shrink it to a single machine, a single room, a single shelf, and you inherit a validated problem
sized for a semester. You also inherit something rarer: the discovery, which tends to stay with
people, that the distance between a course project and a real industry is mostly a matter of scale,
not of kind.
    Instrument a devotion. Hobbies are problems folks have volunteered for: fermentation, aquari-
ums, climbing training, beekeeping, film-developing chemistry, model rocketry. Devotees make the
best users, for three reasons that matter to your grade. They already measure things by hand, so the
value of automating the measurement is pre-established. They will actually run your device. And
they will tell you (at length and for free) exactly what it gets wrong, which is the most expensive
kind of feedback in all of engineering; that is now available here for the price of listening.
    Whatever you find, run it through the guardrails of Section 3 as filters, and through Section 5
as a reality check. Ideally before the memo. Certainly before the design document.

4.2 Seed 1: “Is my elderly parent okay today?” (ambient wellness monitor)
The user is an adult child who lives an hour, or a continent, away from a parent who lives alone.
The moment the product exists for is a quiet one: not the fall, but the morning that didn’t follow

4.3 Seed 2: “Why does my sourdough / homebrew / greenhouse keep failing?”
    (environmental coach)
The user is a devotee (Section 4.1, third method) whose batches keep dying and who has already
tried the obvious: a thermometer that’s glanced at while awake. The insight the product is built on
is that what kills the batch is almost never the moment anyone is looking. It’s the 4 a.m. excursion.
The slow weekend drift. The heater that quietly began short-cycling on Tuesday. And the user’s
real question is never “what is the temperature?”; it’s “what is wrong?” The distance between those
two questions, between a reading and a diagnosis, is exactly the distance your intelligence has to
cover. No threshold covers it.
    Engineering: temperature/humidity plus light or CO2 , sampled at rates that differ by an order of
magnitude, flowing through a storage layer of your own design (D), often behind a no-drop pipeline
(F). The intelligence is rolling statistics, rate-of-change detection, and, the satisfying part, signature
detection. A short-cycling heater oscillates with a period and amplitude you can measure. A failing
seal shows up as indoor humidity coupling to the outdoor weather. A dying yeast culture flattens
a CO2 curve that should be climbing. Encoding that physics into diagnostic rules requires actually
learning the domain. Which means talking to your user, which is the job. Where it bites: the
temptation to promise twelve diagnoses and deliver them all vaguely. Three diagnoses, each with a
measured true- and false-positive rate against failure episodes you provoked on purpose, is the far
stronger project. And Section 5 is about why provoking them on purpose is not a workaround but
a method.

4.4 Seed 3: “Did something happen while I was gone?” (explainable security
    node)
Everyone with a door has asked the question. The commercial answer is four hours of footage
nobody will ever watch. This product’s differentiator is one word: explainable. It answers with a
timeline (3:12 p.m., something person-sized, eleven seconds, moving away) that a human can read
in five seconds and interrogate afterward. The user is anyone who wants that answer without
becoming a security-camera hobbyist and, not incidentally, without pointing an internet-connected
lens at their own life. Like Seed 1, the absence of a camera is a feature you can defend out loud.
     Engineering: PIR motion plus ultrasonic ranging in an interrupt-driven pipeline. That’s mech-
anism B, with the polling comparison built into your evaluation, and usually C, because ranging
an object during a two-second event is a latency budget you have to actually meet rather than
merely admire. The intelligence is fusion (motion says something, range says how big and how
far ), debouncing, event segmentation, and the design of the timeline itself. A log schema from
which a human can reconstruct the truth is a genuine engineering artifact, and it’s the thing your
demo-day answer to “was that the cat?” will be read from. Speaking of the cat: it is this seed’s
honest adversary, and a magnetic reed switch on the door is the cheapest ground-truth generator
you will ever wire. Every real entry gets a free label. Scoped-down version: three event classes
(person-sized, small, unknown) classified honestly, with the confusion matrix to prove it, beats ten
classes classified wishfully.

one compressor, the makerspace with one 3-D printer, the laundromat, the house with a furnace

5 Building in an Imperfect World
Somewhere between the memo and the checkpoint, every team hits the same wall. It’s worth telling
you now that the wall is scheduled. The sensor your design really wants is a $400 thermal imager
and your budget is $60. The $4 accelerometer you bought instead has a noise floor sitting exactly
where the interesting signal lives. The CO2 sensor needs three minutes to warm up and drifts with
the weather. And the data you need at the scale you want (a year of failing compressors, a winter of
greenhouse nights, 104 labeled door events) does not exist, can’t be bought, and won’t be gathered
in one semester by one device on one shelf. None of this means you chose the wrong project! It
means the project has become real. Engineering has been called the art of the possible. The phrase
is not a consolation; it’s the job description. The constraints are not in the way of the work. They
are the medium the work is done in.
    The unproductive response is to stare at what can’t be done. The productive one is to ask,
repeatedly and in roughly this order, what can:
• Substitute. Downgrade the sensor; keep the problem. A PIR and a door switch see more of a
  household’s rhythm than you’d guess a thermal camera was needed for. A microphone’s RMS
  level is a serviceable occupancy proxy. And two cheap sensors that corroborate each other
  routinely outperform one expensive one standing alone. Notice that “corroborate each other” is
  Section 3.1 arriving early, wearing a budget. Record in the design document what you wanted,
  what you used, and what the substitution costs in capability.
• Make your own ground truth. You can’t wait for the bearing to fail, so you provoke the conditions
  and label the recordings: the taped washer, the loosened bolt, the greenhouse vent propped open

• Replay. Build a harness that feeds recorded sensor streams through your real pipeline at real or

    What this means for your grade deserves to be said without hedging: the term project does
not expect a perfect project. It expects an honest one that works. We grade your reasoning
about constraints, never the absence of constraints, because the absence of constraints is not a
condition that occurs in nature. The design document has a home for this reasoning (Section 8),
and the evaluation report’s limitations section is where it pays off. The team that writes “we wanted
X, we could afford Y, and here is precisely what Y cost us” has demonstrated the exact judgment
this course exists to build, and will be graded like it. The team that quietly papers over the gap has
converted an ordinary constraint (the most ordinary thing in engineering) into an integrity problem.
And that is the worst trade available anywhere in this course. We live in an imperfect world. Every
system you will ever ship will ship into it. So you may as well learn to do it well, and without
apology, now.

9 The Evaluation Report (M5)
Adjectives are not measurements. Your evaluation report (3–4 pages, submitted with the final
system) must contain, at minimum:
• Latency or timing, wherever your design claims it matters: distributions (not just means) for
  event-to-detection or sample-to-storage, measured under both idle and loaded CPU.
• Resource footprint: CPU utilization and RSS for each process, at steady state and over the full
  soak (the soak heartbeats give you this series for free; plot it).
• One domain metric: detection accuracy against ground truth you constructed, sustained sample
  rate with drop accounting, or query latency over the stored history. Pick the one your product
  lives or dies by.
• Fault-injection results: for each failure mode in your design-doc table, what you injected, what
  the system did, and the log excerpt proving it.
• The mechanism comparisons your menu choices require (e.g., interrupt vs. polling for item B, RT
  vs. default scheduling for item C), presented as experiments with method, data, and conclusion.
• Limitations, stated plainly, closing the loop on the constraints and substitutions declared in your
  design document (Section 5). An honest limitations section is worth more at the defense than a
  suspiciously perfect results section, and we notice which one we are reading.
   Claude Code can generate plausible code. But it can’t fake your understanding of your own
measurements. Which is why the defense draws so heavily on this report.

17 Hardware Notes
• Boards. Any Raspberry Pi with the 40-pin header works. A Pi 4 or 5 is the comfortable choice;
  a Zero 2 W is fine for the deployed device but slow to compile on, so develop on something larger
  or cross-compile.
• GPIO is 3.3 V and unforgiving. The Pi has no 5 V-tolerant inputs and no analog inputs at all.
  The HC-SR04’s echo pin needs a voltage divider; analog sensors need an ADC (an MCP3008
  over SPI is the classic answer, and SPI is a fine thing to have met). Wire with the power off. A
  Pi killed by a hot-plugged jumper in Week 13 is a schedule event, not a hardware event.
• Power and storage are design inputs. Brownouts corrupt SD cards, and SD cards wear. Your
  storage layer’s fsync discipline, write batching, and recovery story (Section 3.2, item D) are
  not academic. The soak test runs on this exact hardware.
• Budget. Plan on roughly $50–80 per team including the Pi if you own nothing; individual sensors
  run $3–15.

never that tidy.
    But hold this next paragraph together with the previous one, because they are not in tension:
understand what is not being demanded of you. The device you ship in Week 15 will be smaller
than the one you imagined in Week 5. A sensor will have been substituted, a feature cut, a claim
narrowed. The enclosure will be a food container. One graph in your evaluation will end in a shrug.
Good. That shrinkage, honestly accounted for, is not the project failing. It’s the project working,
because it’s the exact shape of every real system you will ever ship. Perfection is not on the rubric
and never was. What is on the rubric is a device that runs, numbers that are real, limitations
that are named, and two people who can each explain the distance between what they wanted to
build and what they built. The teams that struggle here are almost never the ones facing the most
constraints. They are the ones who spend the semester mourning the project they couldn’t do
instead of building the one they could. Don’t join them. When the ideal sensor turns out not to
exist at your budget, or the data you need refuses to exist at your scale, the assignment at that

A Sensor Starter List
Quick flag: anything marked (!) has 5V lurking in it somewhere, so treat those interfaces with a
little extra respect.
     Here’s the thing about the Pi’s GPIO pins: they only speak 3.3V logic, and there’s zero over-
voltage protection built in. Feed one a 5V signal directly and it can just... die. Silently. No warning
light, no smoke, sometimes not even a clue until you notice nothing’s responding anymore. And
sometimes it doesn’t stop at the pin, it takes the whole SoC down with it. That’s exactly why the
HC-SR04 needs a voltage divider on its echo line. The trigger pin is fine with 5V, but the echo pin is
not, and if you wire them the same way because “eh, they’re both just signal pins,” congratulations,
you’ve found the single most popular way to lose a Pi in Week 13.
     But power-rail mistakes are even less forgiving. Swap VCC and GND, or let a 5V rail touch the
3.3V rail while you’re poking around with a multimeter, and your board usually doesn’t warn you
first. It just stops working. No gradual decline, no second chances.
     So here’s the move: build anything 5V-adjacent on a breadboard first. Check your voltages
with a meter before the Pi ever gets plugged in. And always, always wire things up with the board
powered off.
     None of this is meant to be a hard boundary, think of it more as a floor. Weird, exotic sensors
are still welcome at the table, as long as the guardrails hold.

# <project-name>: team rules

## Commands
- Build: ‘make‘        Cross/deploy: ‘make deploy PI=pi@<host>‘
- Tests: ‘make test‘   Sanitizers: ‘make asan‘   Valgrind: ‘make memcheck‘
- Soak sanity: ‘make soakcheck‘ (1-hour miniature of the 48h run)
- A change is DONE only when build, test, and asan pass. Show output.

## Hard constraints
- The PRODUCT makes no network calls except serving its own LAN
  interface. No LLM APIs, no cloud inference, no pretrained models.
  The intelligence in analysis/ is ours. This is a graded boundary.
- Every daemon must be supervisable: clean exit codes, no orphaned
  fds across restart, heartbeat within 60s of start.
- Every allocation checked; every syscall’s error path handled and
  logged. The 48-hour soak is the test suite of last resort.
- NEVER weaken, skip, or delete a test to make the suite pass.

## Ownership
- alice/: capture pipeline, kernel-facing code (src/capture, src/drv)
- bob/:   storage layer, analysis engine (src/store, src/analysis)
- Shared: supervisor, interface. The agent edits outside the current
  session owner’s area only when told explicitly whose session this is.

## Style
- Systems core: C17, -Wall -Wextra -Werror, no VLAs.
  goto-cleanup for multi-resource functions.
- Python permitted only under tools/ and ui/. No graded mechanism
  may live there.
- Smallest diff that passes. Do not refactor unrelated code.

## Workflow
- Multi-file or algorithmic change: plan first, wait for approval.
- Hardware bugs: paste real evidence (dmesg, timing capture,
  /proc/interrupts). No fixes proposed from a verbal description.
- Commit only from a green state; message format "M<n>: <what>".
